ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Cleveland, OH
ut.description: UT inspection and ultrasonic thickness testing in Cleveland, OH for steel mill equipment, piping, vessels, tanks, cranes and structures. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Testing in Cleveland, Ohio
ut.html:
Cleveland runs on heavy steel, and ultrasonic testing (UT) is how owners keep track of what is happening inside it. Atlantis NDT sends technicians to Cleveland mills, terminals, chemical plants and fabrication shops for ultrasonic thickness gauging and for shear-wave examination of welds. Work follows a written procedure and the code your contract names, and the report shows readings and indications you can use in an inspection or repair decision. Start with this Cleveland UT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where UT is used in Cleveland

Steelmaking defines the city's industrial landscape. Cleveland Works, on the Cuyahoga River, is an integrated mill with two blast furnaces, steel-producing vessels with continuous casters, a hot strip mill, a pickle line, a tandem mill and a hot-dip coating line. Equipment of that kind is wall-loss territory: furnace and stove shells, gas and water mains, cooling piping, ladles and casting equipment, and the process piping around pickling, where acid attacks steel from the inside. Hot-blast and gas systems also see cracking concerns that thickness readings alone cannot settle, which is why weld and shell examination often accompanies a survey.

The Port of Cleveland adds a second cluster. Its general cargo terminal handles steel, heavy machinery and wind-energy components with mobile harbor cranes and rail connections, and the Cleveland Bulk Terminal moves iron ore, limestone and cement with an automated ship loader that can serve vessels up to a thousand feet long. Cranes, loader structures, hoppers, conveyor frames and bulk storage all need thickness checks on corroded steel and weld examination on repaired members. Beyond the lakefront, northeast Ohio has chemical, coatings and specialty process plants, power generation along the lake shore, many movable bridges over the Cuyahoga River and highway steel that sits under state DOT programs.

What UT finds and what it misses

The principle is simple. A probe pushes a short burst of sound into the steel, and the instrument measures how long the echo takes to come back and how strong it is. The delay gives thickness; an echo that arrives early or in the wrong place signals a flaw inside the metal. UT therefore measures remaining wall on a corroding pipe, finds laminations in plate, and detects planar flaws in welds such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks, all hidden below the surface.

It has blind spots, and they are not exotic. Sound will not cross a poorly coupled surface, so scale, blistered coating and deep pits have to be dressed first. Cast and coarse-grained material scatters the beam. Round pores and slag can reflect only weakly from the angles used for shear waves, and small or tightly curved parts leave no room for a clean setup. Rolled plate can contain laminations that shadow the weld beneath them, so a technician scans the base metal beside the weld before angle-beam work. These limits go into the report so the engineer knows exactly what the data does and does not cover.

Gauging wall thickness on mill and process equipment

Thickness gauging for code work uses ASME Section V Article 23 (SE-797) or the owner's own procedure. The technician verifies the instrument on a step block of matching material, confirms zero and velocity, and measures along a marked grid or at the owner's condition monitoring locations (CMLs). Dual-element probes handle rough and corroded surfaces, and the A-scan is read directly so that a doubled echo on thin steel is not mistaken for a good wall. On hot piping the technician uses a high-temperature probe and couplant, and corrects for temperature.

In a steel plant the extra factors are heat, scale and access. A line that runs hot in service may be cooled for a short window or measured hot with correction; scale and refractory dust must be cleared before any reading counts. Readings are matched to the CML numbers in the owner's database, or to a numbered grid when there is none, so that corrosion rates can be calculated between campaigns. Where a point cannot be reached, it is logged as not measured rather than skipped quietly.

Weld examination with angle beams

For welds, the technician uses angle-beam probes, commonly 45, 60 and 70 degrees, and scans from both sides when the geometry allows. The reference sensitivity is set from side-drilled holes in a calibration block or taken from the code, and every indication is evaluated against it, then plotted by length, depth and position along the weld. Typical Cleveland scopes include repaired vessel and tank welds, crane runway and structural groove welds, plate and pipe joints on fabricated equipment, and weld repairs on bridge members.

When the owner and the code permit ultrasonic examination in place of radiography, the decision is documented before work begins, with the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector involved. UT does not examine the weld surface itself, and it does not replace magnetic particle or penetrant testing for surface cracks, so a thorough weld scope often includes both.

Codes and state rules for Cleveland UT work

Technique comes from ASME Section V: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials and Article 23 for thickness. Acceptance depends on what you own. Vessels use ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, process piping uses ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.6 with Table 341.3.2, power piping uses ASME B31.1, structural steel uses AWS D1.1 Clause 8 (2020 edition), and bridge steel uses AWS D1.5. In-service pressure equipment follows API 510, API 570 or API 653, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis delivers the examination data: thickness at CMLs, flaw indications and the technique behind them.

Ohio regulates boilers and unfired pressure vessels through the Boiler Section of the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Ohio Department of Commerce, under Chapter 4104 of the Revised Code and Chapter 4101:4 of the Administrative Code, and requires equipment to be built, maintained, altered and repaired to ASME and National Board Inspection Code requirements. Inspectors in Ohio hold a certificate of competency under section 4104.07. Federal OSHA covers private-sector employers in Ohio, so process safety management at covered chemical and refining sites follows 29 CFR 1910.119, including mechanical integrity inspection. See the Ohio inspection services page for the wider state picture.

Who performs the work

Atlantis has no office in Cleveland. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and they are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician calibrates, performs the examination and interprets results; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. The Level III review comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Plants with a procedure of their own can have it applied, and Level III consulting can review it before the crew arrives.

What a Cleveland UT report contains

Expect the component or line identification, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probes, calibration block and calibration checks, the surface condition and temperature, and the technician's name and certification level. A thickness report includes a grid or CML table with nominal, prior and current readings and flags any point under the minimum. A weld report lists each reportable indication with position, depth, length and amplitude, gives the accept or reject decision against the named code, and includes a sketch. Coverage limits, such as one-sided access, are recorded.

Planning a UT job in Cleveland

Lake Erie shapes the calendar. Winter brings snow, ice and wind off the lake, with surfaces that are frozen or wet; cold couplant thickens, batteries fade and outdoor piping and tank shells need to be cleared of ice before a reading counts. Humid summers produce condensation on cold lines and long, hot days in vessels. Because industrial work in the region peaks around plant outages, scopes that need a crew mobilized should be raised with the owner's turnaround team as early as possible.

Site access in Cleveland is rarely casual. Steel plants, marine terminals and chemical sites require orientation, badging and permits, and the port requires credentials at its gates. Tank and vessel entry means confined-space procedures. Crews arrive through Cleveland Hopkins airport or by road across Ohio, and travel is part of the scope. Scaffolding, insulation removal and surface preparation are normally the owner's job, so sort those out beforehand and the crew spends its time measuring instead of waiting.

UT, MT or PT for your Cleveland job

Pick by the flaw. Internal flaws and wall loss belong to UT. A surface crack in carbon steel is better found by magnetic particle inspection in Cleveland, and a surface crack in stainless steel or aluminum by liquid penetrant testing in Cleveland. Weld jobs often combine UT for depth and internal soundness with one of the surface methods. The national ultrasonic testing page and the ultrasonic testing guide explain the method in more depth.

Training your own UT technicians

Companies that want in-house capability can train through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training. Theory runs online, the Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator gives practice, and the practical is completed at the employer's facility under its written practice, with the employer certifying the technician. Details are on the Cleveland NDT training page.

faq.q: Can you do ultrasonic thickness gauging at a Cleveland plant or terminal?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to the site with dual-element probes, step blocks and the right couplant, then measure on a grid or at your monitoring locations and report readings against minimum thickness.

faq.q: Is UT suitable for steel mill piping and shells?
faq.a: Yes, with attention to heat and scale. Hot surfaces need high-temperature probes and correction, scale and refractory dust must be removed, and readings are logged against location IDs so corrosion rates can be tracked.

faq.q: Which UT codes are used on Cleveland welds?
faq.a: Technique follows ASME Section V Article 4, and acceptance follows the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel, or AWS D1.5 for bridges.

faq.q: How does Ohio regulate pressure vessel inspection?
faq.a: Ohio's Division of Industrial Compliance administers boiler and unfired pressure vessel rules under Revised Code Chapter 4104 and Administrative Code 4101:4, applying ASME and National Board requirements. Ask your inspection group which equipment is covered.

faq.q: Does cold lake weather stop ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: It slows it and changes the setup. Cold-rated couplant, protected instruments and ice-free surfaces are needed, and some jobs call for enclosures. Plan winter outdoor scopes with extra care for access and safety.

faq.q: Does UT replace radiography on welds in Cleveland?
faq.a: Only if the code and owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each address ultrasonic examination, so the substitution is agreed in writing in advance with the owner and the authorized inspector.

faq.q: What are the limits of ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Poor coupling, cast or coarse-grained metal, very thin sections and tight geometry reduce reliability, and round porosity may reflect weakly. Surface cracks are better found by MT or PT, and limits are stated in the report.

faq.q: Who qualifies your UT technicians?
faq.a: They are qualified under the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews the reports.

faq.q: How do I request UT in Cleveland?
faq.a: Send the equipment list, applicable code, access details and dates through the quote link on this page. We reply within one business day and confirm scope, procedure and mobilization.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Testing & MPI in Cleveland, OH | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection in Cleveland, OH for welds, crane hooks, shafts, bridge steel and mill equipment. On-site MT to code. Request a quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Cleveland, Ohio
mt.html:
Heavy equipment in Cleveland sees hard service, and fatigue cracks in it start on the surface. Atlantis NDT provides on-site magnetic particle inspection (MPI) for Cleveland welds, crane and rigging hardware, shafts, castings, forgings and steel structures, using yokes, prods or wet fluorescent particles as the job requires. A technician works to a written procedure and reports every relevant indication against the criteria that apply. To start, fill in the Cleveland MT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where magnetic particle testing is used in Cleveland

The city's steel heritage still sets the pattern. At an integrated mill on the Cuyahoga River, MT suits cranes and ladle handling gear, hooks and sheave blocks, roll chocks, couplings, shafts and gearbox parts, and the weld repairs that follow any breakdown. Runway girders and support steel in mill buildings carry moving loads all day, and a toe crack at a weld or a fatigue crack at a bracket corner is exactly the kind of defect MT can reveal before it travels.

Along the lakefront, the Port of Cleveland handles steel, heavy machinery and wind-energy components on its general cargo terminal, and iron ore, limestone and cement at the bulk terminal. Mobile harbor cranes, ship loader structures, hoppers and conveyor frames all contain welded carbon steel under cyclic load. Northeast Ohio also has forges, foundries and fabricators that make castings, structural frames and pressure equipment, and the region's movable bridges over the Cuyahoga rely on large steel shafts, trunnions and gearing, where a crack can take a span out of service. Welding is part of the area's industrial identity, so weld repair verification is a constant need.

What MT finds and what it misses

MT relies on the way a crack disturbs a magnetic field. When a steel part is magnetized, a surface crack or a flaw just beneath the surface forces some of the field out into the air, and iron particles scattered on the part collect there, drawing the crack as a clear line. Under ultraviolet light, fluorescent particles make the line glow and bring out very fine cracks. The method finds cracks, laps, seams and some lack-of-fusion at the surface of a weld.

It will not examine austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or copper alloys, because they do not hold a magnetic field. It will also miss any crack that runs in the same direction as the field, which is why the part is magnetized twice, at roughly right angles. Thick paint or rust reduces sensitivity, and abrupt changes in geometry can produce false-looking lines that must be distinguished from real ones. It tells you where a crack is, not how deep it goes, so deep cracks are followed up by ultrasonic testing or controlled grinding.

How the examination is carried out

The technician begins by confirming the surface is dry and clean and that coatings are thin enough, or removed, so the field can reach the steel. For a field job the AC yoke is the usual tool, and Article 7 of ASME Section V calls for at least 10 lb of lifting power at the pole spacing used for an AC yoke, and 40 lb for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke. Before the job, the yoke is checked on a test weight. Dry powder in a contrasting color is sprayed or dusted while the field is on, and wet particles in a suspension are sprayed when higher sensitivity is wanted.

The technician then examines the surface under adequate white light, or under ultraviolet light in a darkened area for fluorescent work, marks and records each indication, and turns the yoke by about ninety degrees to repeat the examination. For parts that will return to service in a rotating or welded assembly, the residual field is measured and removed by demagnetization if it would cause trouble. Finally, particles are cleaned away and any marking is removed. The written procedure sets each of these points so the examination is the same on every shift.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Cleveland MT work

Technique for code work is ASME Section V Article 7, supported by ASTM E1444 and ASTM E709. Acceptance depends on the part: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural welds and AWS D1.5 for bridge welds. Castings, forgings and lifting equipment use their own product or equipment standards. For in-service pressure equipment, API 510, API 570 and API 653 apply, and the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection while Atlantis reports the examination results.

In Ohio, boilers and unfired pressure vessels fall under the Boiler Section of the Division of Industrial Compliance in the Ohio Department of Commerce, governed by Chapter 4104 of the Revised Code and Chapter 4101:4 of the Administrative Code, with ASME and National Board Inspection Code requirements for repair and alteration. Repair welds on a registered vessel are the sort of work where MT results can end up in an inspector's file. The Ohio inspection page covers the state context in more detail.

Who does the work

There is no Atlantis office in Cleveland. Technicians travel to the site, working under the company's written practice that follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians perform and interpret, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Level III review comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your plant has its own procedure, the crew follows it, and written practice development is available if you need one written or updated.

What the MT report contains

The report identifies the part or weld, the procedure and revision, the technique and equipment, and the particle type and carrier. It records yoke lifting-power checks, light or ultraviolet intensity checks where required, surface condition and temperature, and the technician and level. Each indication is described by location and size, with an accept or reject decision against the named criteria; non-relevant indications are noted with the reason. Photos or sketches locate the findings, and areas that could not be examined are listed so nobody assumes full coverage.

Planning an MT job in Cleveland

Weather off Lake Erie is the first planning item. Cold, wet steel in winter can be below the range a standard procedure covers, wet particle suspensions behave differently, and snow, ice and lake wind complicate outdoor setup; heated enclosures or a low-temperature procedure may be needed. In summer, hot surfaces dry the carrier too quickly and humid air leaves condensation on cold equipment. Fluorescent work needs shade or a tent, which can be hard on open dock and mill yard locations.

Access is the second. Mills, terminals and chemical plants require orientation, permits and sometimes hot-work or confined-space procedures, and the port has credentialed gates. Surface preparation, insulation removal and scaffolding are normally the owner's responsibility, so agreeing them early keeps the crew productive. Technicians usually arrive via Cleveland Hopkins airport or by road, and travel is built into the scope.

MT, PT or UT for your Cleveland job

Use MT on carbon and low-alloy steel when the worry is a surface crack. For stainless steel or aluminum, use dye penetrant inspection in Cleveland. When depth or an internal flaw is the question, use UT inspection in Cleveland. Many repair jobs use MT to confirm that a crack is gone and UT to confirm the repair weld. The national MT service page and the magnetic particle testing guide give additional background.

Training your own MT technicians

For in-house capability, MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training cover the theory online, with the practical completed at your facility under your written practice and your own certification of the technician. See the Cleveland NDT training page for the course path, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker to confirm requirements.

faq.q: Do you offer magnetic particle inspection in Cleveland?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your Cleveland plant, terminal or shop and examine welds, hooks, shafts, castings and structural steel with yokes, prods or wet particles, following a written procedure and the code named in your contract.

faq.q: Which Cleveland equipment is typically examined by MT?
faq.a: Common items include crane and rigging hardware, runway girders, roll chocks, shafts, bridge machinery, weld repairs on pressure equipment, and welded carbon steel on terminal cranes and conveyors, always under the code or specification you name.

faq.q: Can MT be used on stainless steel?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not hold a magnetic field, so MT is not suitable. Liquid penetrant testing is the method used for surface cracks on those materials.

faq.q: How is a crack running along the field found?
faq.a: The part is examined twice with the field turned roughly ninety degrees, because ASME Section V Article 7 requires two examinations so cracks lying in any direction are detected at least once.

faq.q: Does cold weather affect magnetic particle testing in Cleveland?
faq.a: Yes. Particle carriers and surfaces have working limits, so winter jobs may need a low-temperature procedure, enclosures or heating, and the surface temperature is recorded in the report.

faq.q: Is demagnetization always required?
faq.a: No. It is required when residual magnetism could interfere with welding, machining, bearings or later operations. The procedure states when it applies, and the residual field is measured and recorded.

faq.q: Can MT size the depth of a crack?
faq.a: No. MT locates a surface or near-surface crack and shows its length. Depth is established by ultrasonic testing or controlled grinding, so the two methods are often combined on repairs.

faq.q: What is Atlantis's role on API 510, 570 or 653 work?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection. Atlantis performs the magnetic particle examination and reports indications, and the inspector uses that information in repair and evaluation decisions.

faq.q: How do I request MT in Cleveland?
faq.a: Send the part or weld list, the code or specification, access conditions and dates through the quote link on this page. We respond within one business day to confirm scope and travel.

pt.title: Liquid Penetrant Testing & Dye Check in Cleveland, OH
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection in Cleveland, OH for stainless, aluminum and alloy welds, castings and machined parts. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Cleveland, Ohio
pt.html:
Some of the most important surface cracks in Cleveland industry are in metals that a magnet cannot help with: stainless steel piping, aluminum parts, nickel alloy components and non-ferrous castings. Atlantis NDT carries out liquid penetrant testing (PT), often called dye penetrant inspection, at Cleveland plants and shops, using visible or fluorescent systems chosen for the material and surface. The work follows a written procedure and reports each indication against the criteria you specify. Send details through this Cleveland PT quote request; we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Cleveland

Northeast Ohio makes a wide range of products from metals other than plain carbon steel. Chemical, coatings and specialty process plants in the region use stainless steel tanks, reactors, heat exchangers and piping, and the welds in them are routinely examined by PT after fabrication or repair. Precision machining shops and suppliers to aerospace and turbine customers handle aluminum, titanium and nickel alloy parts where a surface crack of a few thousandths of an inch can matter. Foundries and forges in the area examine non-ferrous castings and forgings for laps, cold shuts and porosity.

The steel industry has its own PT scopes. At the mill and the port, stainless and alloy components appear in pickling and coating systems, pump and valve bodies, instrument connections and weld overlays, and PT is how surface integrity is checked once a repair weld has been made. Heat exchanger and condenser work, including tube-to-tubesheet welds and nozzle connections, produces more. Where carbon steel welds have been ground out to remove a crack, PT can serve as an independent check that the excavation is clean when magnetic particle work is impractical.

What PT finds and what it misses

The method is built on capillary action. A low-viscosity liquid carrying a dye is applied to a clean surface and left to soak into any opening. After the excess is removed, a fine developer powder draws the trapped liquid back to the surface where it stains the developer, making a fine crack look like a bold line. PT detects cracks, laps, seams, cold shuts and open porosity, on any non-porous material, magnetic or not.

The weakness is also the strength: PT sees only what is open to the surface. A crack closed by peening, smeared metal from grinding, paint, oil or corrosion product shows nothing, and a rough surface traps penetrant and fills the field with background. Subsurface flaws never show. PT is also a poor choice for porous materials, because the penetrant soaks into the body of the part. It gives the length and position of a surface-breaking flaw and nothing about depth, which is why a cracked part may be followed by ultrasonic measurement or controlled removal.

Technique: from pre-clean to examination

A typical field procedure uses a solvent-removable visible penetrant with a nonaqueous developer, because it is portable, works without a wash station and needs no darkened area. Fluorescent penetrant, examined under ultraviolet light, gives higher sensitivity and is used in shop settings and on critical components. Each product family comes from one manufacturer, and the batch numbers go into the record. The steps are the same every time: clean and dry, apply penetrant, wait for the dwell time, remove excess carefully, apply developer, wait for development, then examine under proper light.

Temperature is part of the technique. ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard range for part and materials at 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and a procedure used outside that range must be qualified at the actual temperature. For stainless steel and nickel alloys, the penetrant, remover and developer are chosen with low halogen and sulfur content, and residues are removed afterward so that they do not contribute to corrosion in service. A reference panel with known cracks proves the system on the day of the job.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Cleveland PT work

ASME Section V Article 6 governs technique for code work, supported by ASTM E165 and ASTM E1417. Acceptance depends on the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, and the relevant structural or product standard for other parts. In-service equipment follows API 510, API 570 or API 653, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis supplies the penetrant examination data.

Ohio's Boiler Section, part of the Division of Industrial Compliance at the Ohio Department of Commerce, enforces Chapter 4104 of the Revised Code and Chapter 4101:4 of the Administrative Code, and requires boilers and unfired pressure vessels to be repaired and altered to ASME and National Board Inspection Code rules. A stainless vessel repair is the kind of job where PT results become part of the record an inspector reviews. For federally covered chemical sites, 29 CFR 1910.119(j) calls for mechanical integrity inspection to good engineering practice. The Ohio inspection services page adds state context.

Reading indications correctly

Developer makes everything that holds penetrant visible, so interpretation is where skill counts. A real crack appears as a sharp, continuous line that keeps bleeding as the developer dries. Porosity shows as rounded dots and a lap as a short curved trace. A mark from a sharp corner, a rough weld toe or leftover penetrant is not a defect, and the technician confirms by wiping the spot with a swab and watching whether it returns. Every doubtful mark is dealt with this way and the result is written down, so the report distinguishes confirmed defects from cleaning artifacts.

Who does the work

Atlantis has no office in Cleveland. Technicians travel to your plant or shop and work to the company's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians prepare, perform, interpret and report, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews results. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Oversight comes from Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If a customer specification or a plant procedure applies, the crew can follow it, and Level III consulting can check the paperwork before work starts.

What the PT report contains

The report lists the part or weld ID, the procedure and revision, the penetrant type and method, the manufacturers and batch numbers of the penetrant, remover and developer, and the pre-cleaning method. It records part temperature, dwell and development times, lighting conditions, and the technician and level. Indications are described by position, length and form with an accept or reject decision, and photographs or sketches locate them. Areas that could not be prepared or examined are noted, as are doubtful marks that were re-examined.

Planning a PT job in Cleveland

Lake Erie weather matters more for PT than for most methods. Winter steel and aluminum can sit well below the 40 degree floor, where penetrant thickens and dwell behavior shifts, so cold-weather work needs a qualified procedure, tents or heaters, or warming of the part. Summer sun on a dock or a tank can push surface temperature above the top of the range and dry the penetrant too fast. Wind-blown dust, road salt and lake moisture all find their way onto surfaces and have to be cleaned off.

Before the crew mobilizes, agree on surface preparation, coatings, insulation, scaffolding and access, which are normally the owner's responsibility. Plants may specify chemical restrictions for stainless and nickel work, so penetrant materials and clean-up are usually approved in advance. Orientation, permits and port credentials apply as for any contractor, and technicians travel to Cleveland by air through Hopkins or by road, with travel built into the scope.

PT, MT or UT for your Cleveland job

Choose PT for non-magnetic metals and for surface cracks where a magnet is awkward. For carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Cleveland is usually faster and also shows flaws just below the surface. For wall loss or internal flaws, ultrasonic testing in Cleveland is the right tool. See the national penetrant testing page for general information on the method.

Training your own PT technicians

If your own people will do penetrant work, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training provide the theory online, the Practical NDT penetrant simulator gives practice, and the hands-on part takes place at your facility under your written practice, with your company certifying the technician. The Cleveland NDT training page sets out the path.

faq.q: Do you provide liquid penetrant testing in Cleveland?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your Cleveland plant or shop and examine welds, castings, forgings and machined parts for surface-breaking flaws, using visible or fluorescent penetrant to a written procedure and the code named in your contract.

faq.q: What materials can be examined with dye penetrant?
faq.a: Any non-porous material: stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, carbon steel, many ceramics and some plastics. It cannot be used on porous materials, and it shows only flaws open to the surface.

faq.q: Why are some penetrants specified for stainless and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Those alloys can be harmed in service by halogen or sulfur residues. Low-halogen and low-sulfur materials are chosen for them, and the part is cleaned after examination. Batch certificates are kept with the record.

faq.q: Can PT be done outdoors in Cleveland winters?
faq.a: Only with a procedure qualified for the actual temperature. The standard ASME Section V Article 6 range is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, so cold outdoor work normally needs heaters, tents or a low-temperature qualification.

faq.q: How do you tell a real indication from a false one?
faq.a: A real crack shows as a sharp line that keeps bleeding as developer dries. Doubtful marks are wiped with a swab and observed again, and the result is recorded so the report separates defects from cleaning artifacts.

faq.q: What surface preparation is needed before PT?
faq.a: The surface must be clean, dry and free of paint, oil, scale and smeared metal that could close a crack. Grinding and machining sometimes require etching, and the owner normally arranges coating removal and access.

faq.q: Can PT replace MT on carbon steel?
faq.a: It can find surface cracks there, but MT is usually quicker and also shows flaws just below the surface. PT is chosen when magnetizing is impractical or the owner's specification calls for it.

faq.q: Who inspects pressure equipment in Ohio?
faq.a: Ohio's Division of Industrial Compliance oversees boilers and unfired pressure vessels under Revised Code Chapter 4104. Atlantis performs the penetrant examination, and the owner's inspector and the state rules decide how results are used.

faq.q: How do I request PT in Cleveland?
faq.a: Send the component list, the code or specification, the materials involved and your dates through the quote link on this page. We reply within one business day and confirm scope, materials and travel.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing Alternatives in Cleveland, OH | RT
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Cleveland, UT, ASNT Level III review of radiographs and RT training are available. Ask for a quote.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Cleveland, Ohio: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, including in Cleveland. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity governed by Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules (10 CFR Part 34) or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and Atlantis does not provide it. If you came here looking for radiography in northeast Ohio, this page explains the related work Atlantis can do and how to scope it.

UT as the volumetric alternative on Cleveland welds

Many of the questions people try to answer with radiography, such as whether a weld has lack of fusion, slag or cracking, can also be addressed by ultrasonic examination where the construction code and the owner permit. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 sets its own acceptance criteria for ultrasonic examination of groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows UT in place of RT only under specific conditions. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job, and it is written into the procedure. On a working mill or terminal, UT has a practical benefit: it needs no exclusion zone, so neighboring crews keep working. The same visit can add magnetic particle inspection in Cleveland or liquid penetrant testing in Cleveland to cover the weld surface.

faq.q: Is radiography part of what Atlantis does in Cleveland?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. Industrial radiography is licensed under NRC rules (10 CFR Part 34) or Agreement State equivalents, and it is not a service we offer in Cleveland.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing stand in for radiography on my welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 provide for ultrasonic examination, but substitution is agreed in advance with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector, then written into the procedure.

faq.q: What radiography-related review can an ASNT Level III do without a source?
faq.a: A Level III can review radiographs and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read on disputed indications and review an RT contractor's procedure and written practice.

faq.q: Can Atlantis name a radiography contractor in Ohio?
faq.a: No. We do not recommend radiography contractors. If your work needs radiography, verify the contractor's license with the state radiation control program and ask to see their written practice and procedures.

faq.q: Can my technicians study radiography theory with Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. The radiographic testing Level 2 course covers theory online. Hands-on exposure depends on licensing and radiation safety training through your employer, which certifies its technicians under SNT-TC-1A.
